subtype: Contempt and ridicule as warning signs [Interpreting]
passage: Varun ran the tea stall by the bus stand in Nitin's village, and for months he had teased Nitin whenever the young man passed on his way to the polytechnic. "Engineer sahib, mind the puddle," he would say with a smirk, and the men on the bench would snort. Nitin used to laugh along. Lately he had stopped. One morning he set down his bag and said, without raising his voice, "Varun-bhai, I've noticed you laugh at me a lot. I'd like you to stop that. I still want to buy my tea here." Varun blinked, and the bench went silent. He wiped a glass slowly. Nitin waited a moment, paid, and walked on. Varun said nothing, but the next day he only said, "Morning, Nitin."

qa.q: What did Varun call Nitin when he teased him?
qa.a: He called him "Engineer sahib".

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when he stopped laughing along, and what might Varun have been feeling in the silence?
qa.a: Nitin was probably tired of being belittled, and Varun may have been embarrassed or surprised, though his blank silence does not prove which.

qa.q: What did Nitin do that was wiser than trading insults?
qa.a: He stated the pattern calmly, set a limit, and made it clear he still wanted to buy his tea there.

qa.q: How might the men on the bench have seen this?
qa.a: They may have been startled, since the teasing had been treated as normal fun, and some may have begun to see how it felt for Nitin.

grounding: Nitin recognises ridicule as disrespect, names it calmly and sets a limit without insults.

subtype: Contempt and ridicule as warning signs [Interpreting]
passage: Jin had been with Oskar for a year in Stockholm when she started noticing something. At dinner with friends, when she told a story about her job at the museum, Oskar rolled his eyes and said, "Here comes another fascinating painting." Everyone laughed. At home, when she cried about her grandmother in Seoul, he sighed loudly: "Drama again." Each time, she laughed it off. But she'd started telling fewer stories. She felt smaller in her own flat. One evening, after he mimicked her accent in front of his cousins, she didn't laugh. At home she said, calmly, "When you mock me or roll your eyes when I talk, I feel disrespected. It keeps happening. I need it to stop." He scoffed. "You can't take a joke." That night Jin called her friend Mina and talked for an hour. The next week she booked a session with a counsellor at the student centre.

qa.q: What did Oskar say when Jin talked about her job at the museum?
qa.a: "Here comes another fascinating painting."

qa.q: What was Jin feeling as the mockery went on?
qa.a: She felt smaller and disrespected, telling fewer stories and laughing things off, until she no longer could.

qa.q: What steps did Jin take that were wise?
qa.a: She named the pattern calmly and set a limit, and when Oskar scoffed, she talked to a friend and booked a counsellor instead of trading insults.

qa.q: How did Oskar see Jin's request?
qa.a: He dismissed it, scoffing that she couldn't take a joke, which suggests he didn't see his mockery as disrespect.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising repeated eye-rolls and mockery in a relationship as contempt, naming it, setting a limit and seeking help.

passage: In the Chennai design office, Neelam, the senior designer, had a habit. When Noor presented an idea, Neelam would smirk, glance at the others and say something like, "Cute. Very college project." Once she rolled her eyes so obviously that the intern giggled. Noor started saying less in meetings. She noticed her hands getting cold before every review. At first she wondered if she was being too sensitive. Then she began writing it down: dates, words, who was there. After the fourth time in a month, she asked Neelam for a word, privately. "When you call my ideas cute and roll your eyes in reviews, it feels like mockery. I'd like feedback on the work instead." Neelam laughed. "Relax." So Noor took her notes to her mentor, Mr Pillai. He read them, frowned and said, "This isn't about sensitivity. I'll raise it with HR and sit in on your next review."

qa.q: What did Neelam say about Noor's ideas?
qa.a: "Cute. Very college project."

qa.q: What was Noor feeling before reviews?
qa.a: She felt anxious, her hands getting cold before every review, and doubted herself, wondering if she was too sensitive.

qa.q: What steps did Noor take that others could copy?
qa.a: She wrote down the incidents, named the pattern calmly to Neelam, and when that failed, took her notes to her mentor for help.

qa.q: How did Mr Pillai respond when Noor showed him her notes?
qa.a: He took it seriously, said it wasn't about sensitivity, and promised to raise it with HR and sit in on her next review.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising sneering and eye-rolls at work as disrespect, naming it calmly and seeking help rather than trading insults.

passage:
Santosh,
We've been friends since Class 6, so I'm going to say this straight, in writing, because when I try to say it out loud you laugh.
For a few months now, whenever I talk about my music, you roll your eyes or put on a squeaky voice and say, "Ooh, the artist." In front of the others too. At first I laughed along. Now I just stop talking. That's not how friends are supposed to feel with each other.
I'm not trying to start a fight or call you names. I'm naming what keeps happening. I'd like it to stop. If you think I've got it wrong, tell me; I'll listen.
If it keeps happening, I'll need to spend less time around you, and I really don't want that.
Still your friend,
Ujjwal

qa.q: How long have Ujjwal and Santosh been friends?
qa.a: Since Class 6.

qa.q: What is Ujjwal feeling about Santosh's mockery?
qa.a: Ujjwal feels hurt and small, having gone from laughing along to simply stopping talking, and is worried about losing the friendship.

qa.q: What makes Ujjwal's letter a wise response?
qa.a: It names the pattern calmly without insults, asks for it to stop, offers to listen, and sets a clear limit.

qa.q: How might Santosh see the squeaky voice compared with Ujjwal?
qa.a: Santosh may think it's harmless teasing, while for Ujjwal it has become mockery that makes Ujjwal stop sharing.

grounding: Shows a young adult recognising repeated mockery and eye-rolls as disrespect, naming it calmly and setting a limit.

passage: You're the first person I'm saying this to properly, Sudha, so bear with me. I'm Kiran, and you know Tushar and I have been together a year. It wasn't one big thing. It was the eye-rolls whenever I talked about my dance classes. The little sneer, "Oh, here's the artist," in front of his friends. Last month I got a question wrong at trivia night and he did this slow clap, and everyone laughed. I laughed too. Then I went to the washroom and couldn't stop shaking. I used to tell myself it was just his humour. But jokes don't leave you feeling small every single time. On Saturday I said calmly, "When you mock my classes or roll your eyes at me, I feel disrespected. I need it to stop." He rolled his eyes again. So on Monday I went to the college counsellor, who helped me think it through. I'm not trading insults with him. I'm deciding what I deserve.
